questions.bookRef: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.explanation: The hash map holds key → byte offset, so values stay on disk and only keys need RAM. Caching just values would still require a disk scan per lookup, a sample of keys defeats O(1) lookup, and whole segments never sit in memory.
options: Every key, mapped to its byte offset in the log
Every key-value pair, so lookups never touch disk
The most recently written log segment
A sample of keys; the rest are found by scanning segments
questions.question: In a log-structured hash index, what must fit entirely in memory?

questions.bookRef: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.explanation: The memtable is a sorted structure, so a full one is written out as a single immutable sorted run (SSTable) and a fresh empty memtable takes over. Page splits are a B-tree mechanism, eviction would lose data, and merging happens later as background compaction — not at flush time.
options: It is flushed to disk as an immutable, sorted SSTable
It is split into two smaller memtables, like a B-tree page split
Its oldest entries are evicted to make room for new writes
It is merged in place with the oldest SSTable on disk
questions.question: In an LSM-tree, what happens when the in-memory memtable fills up?

questions.bookRef: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.explanation: B-trees update pages in place, so a crash can leave torn pages; the WAL records every modification so unflushed changes can be replayed. Memtables, compaction, and hash-map snapshots belong to log-structured engines, not B-trees.
options: By replaying the write-ahead log (redo log) since the last checkpoint
By rebuilding pages from the in-memory memtable
By running compaction to merge all SSTables
By restoring the hash map snapshot taken at startup
questions.question: How does a B-tree recover its on-disk pages to a consistent state after a crash?

questions.bookRef: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.explanation: Full-text search needs term → documents, i.e. an inverted index, which also enables ranking and fuzzy matching. A hash index cannot do prefix or fuzzy queries, and concatenated or clustered indexes organize rows rather than mapping terms to documents.
options: An inverted index mapping each term to the documents containing it
A hash index mapping each document to its keywords
A concatenated multi-column index over (document, term)
A clustered index storing documents sorted by keyword
questions.question: Which index structure powers keyword search over document text?

questions.explanation: OLAP means few, heavy analytic queries over large scans. High volumes of tiny interactive operations, row-by-row updates, and live point lookups are all OLTP patterns.
options: A small number of queries, each scanning or aggregating millions of rows
A huge volume of small interactive reads and writes
Row-by-row updates with strict per-transaction latency
Point lookups serving live user requests
questions.question: Which workload pattern describes OLAP?

questions.explanation: The fact table records events (e.g. sales) as foreign keys into dimensions (who/what/where/when) plus measures (price, quantity). Normalizing dimensions further is the snowflake variant, measures belong in the fact table, and bitmaps are a storage technique — not the fact table's content.
options: One row per event, with foreign keys to dimension tables and numeric measures
Fully normalized dimension attributes with no redundant data
Only primary keys; all measures live in the dimension tables
Precomputed bitmap indexes for every possible query
questions.question: In a star schema, what does the fact table contain?

questions.explanation: Analytics aggregate a few columns over many rows, so columnar layout reads only those columns and slashes I/O. It does not remove the need for indexes, single-row writes are actually harder (hence buffered LSM-style writes), and storing a row's columns together is row-oriented storage — the opposite.
options: Analytic queries usually read only a few columns, so the engine skips loading the rest
It eliminates the need for indexes on analytic tables
Columnar layouts make single-row writes faster
It stores each row's columns together to improve cache locality
questions.question: Why does column-oriented storage speed up typical analytic queries?

questions.bookRef: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.explanation: LSM writes are sequential (memtable append plus SSTable flush), giving write speed, while a B-tree lookup touches one page per key. Compaction rewrites data in the background, stealing I/O from live traffic. B-trees do amplify writes: every update hits the WAL and may rewrite or split pages.
options: LSM-trees typically sustain higher write throughput because writes are sequential
B-trees have lower read amplification because each key lives in exactly one place
LSM-tree compaction consumes disk bandwidth and can interfere with live reads and writes
B-trees never suffer write amplification since pages are updated in place
questions.question: Which statements about LSM-trees versus B-trees are true?

questions.bookRef: Data Structures That Power Your Database
questions.explanation: Clustered means rows live inside the index, and covering means all needed columns are in the index so no heap fetch is required. Concatenated indexes help only queries on a leftmost prefix of the column list (like a phone book sorted by last, then first name), and secondary indexes commonly reference the primary key or heap tuple rather than a stable disk address.
options: In a clustered index, the table row itself is stored within the index
A covering index contains every column a query needs, so the heap/table is never touched
A concatenated multi-column index speeds up queries that filter on any single one of its columns
Secondary index entries always point directly to the row's disk location with no indirection
questions.question: Which statements about index types are true?

questions.explanation: ETL extracts from production systems, cleans and reshapes, then loads into the warehouse; the split exists because OLAP access patterns would hurt OLTP latency and favor denormalized analytic schemas. Warehouses deliberately denormalize into star/snowflake schemas, and transforming is the middle step of ETL — not something pushed back onto OLTP.
options: Data is moved from OLTP systems into the warehouse via ETL: extract, transform, load
Analytics runs separately because heavy analytic queries would degrade OLTP performance and need different schemas
Warehouses keep data in the same highly normalized schema as the OLTP source
ETL pipelines only copy data; all cleaning and reshaping happens inside the OLTP database
questions.question: Which statements about data warehousing are true?

questions.explanation: Bitmap encoding uses one bit per row per distinct value, run-length encoding thrives on sorted runs (e.g. a date-sorted column), and column stores avoid in-place updates by buffering and merging writes. Row-independent compression defeats the purpose: columnar compression works precisely because it exploits similarity across many values in one column.
options: Bitmap encoding represents each distinct value as a bit vector marking the rows that hold it
Run-length encoding compresses well when a column is sorted so equal values form long runs
Writes are buffered in memory and merged into column files LSM-style, because in-place column updates are expensive
Each row is compressed independently to keep single-row lookups fast
questions.question: Which statements about column-oriented storage are true?

questions.explanation: The chapter's two engine families trade write against read optimization, and the workload split (OLTP vs OLAP) is why warehouses and columnar stores exist. OLTP is the interactive one and warehouses are analytic — not vice versa — and every index costs write overhead and disk space.
options: Log-structured engines (hash indexes, LSM-trees) favor write throughput; page-oriented B-trees favor read efficiency
OLTP systems are built for bulk analytic scans, while data warehouses serve interactive transactions
The OLTP/OLAP split motivated separate data warehouses and column-oriented storage for analytics
Indexes speed up reads for free, with no cost to writes or storage
questions.question: Which statements capture this chapter's big picture?

summary.overview: This chapter opens up the database to show how storage engines actually put bytes on disk: log-structured designs (hash indexes, SSTables, LSM-trees) versus page-oriented B-trees, and why each wins on different workloads. It then draws the line between transaction processing (OLTP) and analytics (OLAP), explaining data warehouses, star schemas, and column-oriented storage. For interview prep, this is the chapter that lets you reason about why a database behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box.

sections.heading: Data Structures That Power Your Database
takeaways: A hash index keeps an in-memory map from each key to its byte offset in an append-only log, so all keys — but not values — must fit in RAM.
LSM-trees buffer writes in a sorted in-memory memtable; when it fills, it is flushed as an immutable sorted SSTable, and background merging (compaction) discards overwritten or deleted values.
B-trees store data in fixed-size pages updated in place, and recover from crashes by replaying the write-ahead (redo) log.

LSM-trees win on write throughput via sequential I/O, while B-trees win on read efficiency since each key exists in exactly one place; LSM compaction costs disk bandwidth and can disturb live traffic.

Index flavors matter: clustered indexes store the row inside the index, covering indexes hold every column a query needs, concatenated multi-column indexes help only leftmost-prefix queries, and full-text search uses an inverted index of terms to documents.

sections.heading: Transaction Processing or Analytics?
takeaways: OLTP means huge volumes of small interactive reads and writes; OLAP means a few queries each scanning or aggregating millions of rows.
Data warehouses sit apart from OLTP systems — analytic workloads would hurt production performance and want different schemas — and are fed by ETL (extract, transform, load).
A star schema centers on a fact table (one row per event: foreign keys to dimensions plus numeric measures); snowflake schemas normalize the dimensions further.

sections.heading: Column-Oriented Storage
takeaways: Columnar storage lays each column contiguously, so analytic queries that read few columns touch far less data — and columns compress better because adjacent values are similar.
Bitmap encoding (one bit-vector per distinct value) and run-length encoding (long runs in sorted columns) shrink analytic datasets dramatically.
Sort order powers compression (sorted columns form compressible runs), and writes are buffered in memory then merged into column files LSM-style because in-place column updates are costly.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Two storage-engine families: log-structured (hash indexes, SSTables/LSM-trees) optimized for writes, and page-oriented (B-trees) optimized for reads — choose by workload.
The OLTP/OLAP divide is why data warehouses exist separately from production databases, and why analytics moved to column-oriented storage.
